 A federal judge found immigration authorities in contempt after they released a migrant as ordered and then immediately arrested him again, saying the practice “made a mockery” of court orders requiring detainees’ release. U.S. District Judge Charlotte Sweeney ruled in Colorado on Tuesday that Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officials violated her order to release Ramon Quintero Alvarez by October 28, unless the government showed cause to keep him detained. The Mexico-born father-of-two, who has lived in the U.S. since entering in the early 1990s, had been detained since February. ICE official Nichole Black testified on November 4 that she was ordered to re-detain released detainees with “some type of criminality.” Quintero Alvarez had previously been arrested on criminal charges, but charges stemming from his most recent arrest were dropped on April 24, the papers said without specifying the charges. Sweeney said Black told the court Quintero Alvarez was released and "then 'walked out to the lobby,' exited the detention facility 'into a public area' where 'officers met him outside and rearrested him.'" "Ms. Black said in her own words that she believed it was permissible to simply escort someone to a public area and immediately re-detain them despite a court order to the contrary," the Biden-appointed judge wrote in a 15-page order. “This should—and, in the Court’s opinion, must—shock any reader." Black said she knew of about 10 such cases, a figure the court said was later increased to 18. Sweeney noted that it had an agreement with federal prosecutors requiring the government to carry out the release of detainees in accordance with judges’ orders. "And yet despite—or perhaps in spite—of this memorandum and court orders that have ordered petitioners’ immediate release, the Court observed that Respondents and ICE’s new “policy” of immediately re-detaining petitioners following release made a mockery of court orders mandating petitioners’ immediate release," Sweeney wrote. Newsweek contacted ICE and its parent agency, the Department of Homeland Security, for comment via email outside of regular office hours on Thursday. Black said she had been acting on a “direct order” from deputy field office director George Valdez, who had received an order from acting field office director Nathan Rasper. Rasper testified that he told officials to consult ICE lawyers before re-arresting someone to determine whether another arrest was lawful. He said ICE colleagues in Minnesota had told him people could be re-arrested after being released. Rasper said Black had misunderstood his instructions, which he acknowledged “were not clear.” He said he ordered the office to stop the practice following Black's November 4 testimony and release those who had been re-arrested under it. ‘Any Reader May Be Lost for Words’ Sweeney found Black and the Trump administration in contempt for knowingly disobeying the court’s release order but declined further action. “To recap: civil contempt is appropriate where clear and convincing evidence shows that a valid court order existed—check—Respondents had knowledge of that order—check—and Respondents disobeyed it—check,” Sweeney wrote. “Sometimes, behavior stuns and renders a listener speechless,” Sweeney wrote. “To the extent any reader may be lost for words as to what ICE and Respondents did in this case and others in this judicial district like it—and the ridiculous nature of the justification for their behavior." Federal judges have repeatedly squared off with Trump administration lawyers over the president’s immigration crackdown, including disputes over detention practices and compliance with court orders. In a separate case this month, U.S. District Judge S. Kato Crews ordered the administration to release Edgardo Garcia Vargas after ICE arrested him minutes after his court-ordered release. Crews called the re-arrest an “ongoing due process violation” and warned that another arrest without a hearing could lead to contempt proceedings. The Trump administration has sought to increase immigration arrests and deportations under it's hardline mass deportation campaign. In Colorado, ICE arrests nearly doubled from 259 in March to 499 in July 2026, according to federal data obtained through the Freedom of Information Act by the Deportation Data Project. There were 549 arrests in July 2025.
